headline: Unlikely intersections in abelian varieties are claimed to be finite in number, in every dimension.
scope: The first result covers every subvariety of every abelian variety over the algebraic numbers; the others cover Hodge-generic curves in the Siegel threefold A₂.
plain: An abelian variety is a geometric shape with a way to add its points. A dimension count predicts how big its intersections with special pieces should be. The abelian Zilber–Pink conjecture says the bigger-than-expected intersections fall into finitely many families. The first paper claims to prove it over the algebraic numbers in every dimension. Three more papers claim the curve case in A₂, a space whose points stand for abelian surfaces.
doesNot: This does not bound how many atypical pieces there are, and it does not cover Zilber–Pink in general Shimura varieties.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: B. Zilber, who formulated the unlikely-intersection principle for semiabelian varieties
scorecard.significanceWhy: Earlier results covered curves or added extra conditions; the paper claims every dimension and codimension, if the proof holds.

explanation:
Take the curve y² = x³ − x. Its points, with one extra point at infinity, can be added by a geometric rule. That makes it an elliptic curve, the simplest abelian variety (a shape whose points can be added). The points (0, 0), (1, 0) and (−1, 0) are torsion points. Adding any one of them to itself gives the zero point. Products of such curves give abelian varieties of any dimension.

Inside an abelian variety A, the special pieces are torsion cosets. A torsion coset is a smaller abelian variety shifted by a torsion point[1]. Now take a subvariety X, a curved shape inside A. Dimensions predict how big X meets a special piece T: dim X + dim T − dim A. Take A as a product of three elliptic curves, so dimension 3. Let X be a curve, dimension 1, and T a shifted elliptic curve, dimension 1. The prediction is 1 + 1 − 3 = −1, so they should not meet at all. A meeting point is atypical: bigger than predicted[2].

Such meetings can happen, because the pieces T vary without end. The abelian Zilber–Pink conjecture says they are rare in a precise sense. All the largest atypical pieces fall into a finite list[3]. The case where every T is a single torsion point is the Manin–Mumford theorem, proved by Raynaud in 1983[4]. Zilber stated the general principle in 2002, and Pink gave a related form in 2005[5].

Before this paper, the curve case was known. Habegger and Pila proved finiteness for curves in any abelian variety over number fields in 2016[6]. Barroero, Kühne and Schmidt extended it to semiabelian varieties[7]. In higher dimensions, results needed extra conditions on how X sits under quotient maps[8]. Some covered powers of a single elliptic curve in codimension two[9].

The first paper claims the conjecture over number fields in every dimension[10]. For every abelian variety and every subvariety X, the largest atypical pieces form a finite list[3]. No condition on A is imposed, such as complex multiplication (extra symmetries of the curve)[11]. The theorem gives no bound for how many pieces there are[12]. In the example, a curve in the triple product has only finitely many such atypical meeting points.

The hard part is height. Height measures how complicated the coordinates of a point are. Earlier non-density results held below each fixed height bound[13]. The paper uses a height argument in the tradition of Vojta and Faltings[14]. It adds geometric results of Ax and of Habegger and Pila. It then passes from non-density to finiteness with a reduction by Barroero and Dill[15].

Three companion papers treat curves in A₂ (a space whose points stand for abelian surfaces with a fixed kind of polarization). A curve there is Hodge generic when it lies in no proper special subvariety[16]. One paper claims finiteness for points whose surface is like E × E for a non-CM elliptic curve E[17]. The other two cover products with a CM factor, and quaternion division points[18]. Together they claim the curve case of Zilber–Pink in A₂[19].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for these papers in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked them. The A₂ result depends on all three linked papers. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proofs hold. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. The results are ineffective: they give no bound on how many atypical pieces occur.

glossary.meaning: A geometric shape defined by polynomial equations whose points can be added like numbers.
An abelian variety of dimension one, such as the points of y² = x³ − x plus a point at infinity.
A point that returns to zero after being added to itself some number of times.
A smaller abelian variety shifted by a torsion point; the special pieces in this problem.
An intersection piece of larger dimension than a dimension count predicts.
A measure of how complicated the coordinates of an algebraic point are.
For a curve in A₂, lying in no proper special subvariety.
Extra symmetries of an elliptic curve beyond multiplication by whole numbers.
